Installing torch

Source: vignettes/articles/installation.Rmd
installation.Rmd

The neural networks cnn(), rescnn() and mlp() require torch, a library for training and using neural networks. This article covers installation and checks for running on a central processor (CPU) or graphics processor (GPU). The README describes the default timesift installation. Other learners use timesift’s compiled C++ code.

torch for R is an R package plus two libraries it downloads after installation, LibTorch and LibLantern. torch for Python is one wheel from PyPI or from PyTorch’s own index. The steps below follow the torch for R installation guide and PyTorch’s install page; those pages are the reference when a version here has moved on.

R

Processor and Apple Silicon 

install.packages("torch")
torch::install_torch(timeout = 600)

In an interactive session torch installs the two libraries by itself the first time it is needed; install_torch() does it explicitly, and is what a script or a cluster job runs. A non-interactive session also downloads on load when the environment variable TORCH_INSTALL is 1. On Apple Silicon the same build runs on the graphics processor through MPS.

NVIDIA graphics processor

The simplest route is torch’s pre-built binary, which carries CUDA and cuDNN inside it, so neither has to be installed on the system. It is about 2 GB, hence the longer timeout:

options(timeout = 600)
kind <- "cu128"
version <- available.packages()["torch", "Version"]
options(repos = c(
  torch = sprintf("https://torch-cdn.mlverse.org/packages/%s/%s/", kind, version),
  CRAN = "https://cloud.r-project.org"
))
install.packages("torch")

kind is "cu128" for CUDA on Windows and Linux, "cpu" for the processor build, and "cpu-intel" or "cpu-m1" on macOS.

The alternative is a system CUDA toolkit: version 12.8 on Windows, 12.6, 12.8 or 12.9 on Linux, with a matching cuDNN, then install.packages("torch") as above. Sys.setenv(CUDA = "12.8") before installing forces the version torch looks for. The CUDA runtime can also come as an R package instead of a system toolkit:

install.packages("cuda12.8",
                 repos = c("https://mlverse.r-universe.dev", "https://cloud.r-project.org"))
install.packages("torch")

Checking what torch found 

torch::torch_is_installed()
torch::cuda_is_available()
torch::backends_mps_is_available()

train_control(device = "auto"), the default, takes CUDA where cuda_is_available() is TRUE, MPS where backends_mps_is_available() is, and the processor otherwise. A fit carries the setting rather than the device it resolved to, so a model trained on a GPU machine predicts on a laptop. To pin one device for a whole run:

fit <- timesift(plots, logger, y = starts_with("sp_"), id = plot, time = datetime,
                learners = cnn(), sift = grains("week"),
                control = train_control(device = "cuda"))

When the download fails

  • “Timeout of 60 seconds was reached”: torch::install_torch(timeout = 600).
  • More detail on what failed: Sys.setenv(TORCH_INSTALL_DEBUG = 1) before installing.
  • No internet on the machine, or a blocked download: torch::get_install_libs_url() prints the two URLs. Download both files on a machine that can reach them, copy them over, and point the install at the local copies:
Sys.setenv(TORCH_URL = "/path/to/libtorch.zip")
Sys.setenv(LANTERN_URL = "/path/to/lantern.zip")
torch::install_torch()
  • Windows, a missing lantern.dll module: the Microsoft Visual C++ runtime is missing; the torch installation guide links the fix.

Python

Processor, Apple Silicon and Linux with CUDA 

pip install "timesift[torch]"

The torch extra pulls torch from PyPI. On Linux that wheel brings its CUDA libraries with it, so an NVIDIA graphics processor works without further setup. On macOS it runs on Apple Silicon’s graphics processor through MPS. On Windows it runs on the processor only.

Windows with an NVIDIA graphics processor

Install torch from PyTorch’s own index first, then timesift; pip keeps the torch already there:

pip install torch --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu130
pip install "timesift[torch]"

cu130 is CUDA 13.0; cu126 and cu132 are also published for the current torch. The graphics processor’s driver has to support the CUDA version chosen; nvidia-smi prints the highest one it does. No CUDA toolkit is needed beyond the driver.

Checking what torch found 

python -c "import torch; print(torch.__version__, torch.cuda.is_available())"

On Windows a version without a +cu suffix (such as 2.14.1 rather than 2.14.1+cu130) is the PyPI processor build, and the index step above was skipped. ts.train_control(device="auto") resolves the device as in R.
